claims.text: Thermal-expansion mismatch among Hf, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr generates local stress concentrations in HfNbTaTiZr.
The mismatch-generated local stresses couple with dislocation-mediated plasticity.
Temperature-dependent internal stresses modify dislocation interactions and slip pathways.
This coupling causes anomalous stress-strain and thermoelastic behavior across cold-rolled, aged, and high-temperature-creep conditions.
Nominally equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr is a predominantly single-phase, disordered BCC solid solution with minimal second phases.
The relevant starting condition is as-cast or solution-annealed.
Reducing the Hf or Zr content would alter the alloy's thermal-expansion mismatch.
An inert atmosphere minimizes oxidation effects during high-temperature testing.
Minor atomic clustering or short-range ordering contributes to local stress fields that influence dislocation motion.
Heating or cooling creates elevated local internal stresses because the constituent elements have different thermal expansions.
These internal stresses impede or redirect dislocation glide.
Impeded or redirected glide produces hardening or low-ductility plateaus in specific temperature regimes.
Changes in flow stress and work-hardening with temperature will track measured shifts in internal stress.
Compositions with greater thermal-expansion mismatch, such as higher-Hf variants, will show stronger and earlier strength or ductility anomalies.
Tests without simultaneous thermal-expansion measurements or with narrower temperature windows lack steep internal-stress variations attributable to thermal mismatch.
Below approximately 300 degrees Celsius, ordinary lattice friction dominates slip and mismatch-induced stresses are minimal.
Above approximately 1250 degrees Celsius, creep mechanisms dominate and obscure thermal-mismatch effects.
Small compositional or local-structural changes could shift thermal expansion enough to obscure the proposed mechanism.
The HfNbTaTiZrV0.5 derivative exhibits a low-plasticity plateau between 873 and 1073 K.
A single-BCC refractory HEA exhibits distinctive elastic deformation behavior and phase stability up to 900 degrees Celsius.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis treats mismatch-induced stresses as physical consequences of temperature change, whereas the baseline implies that omitting simultaneous thermal-expansion measurement makes the steep internal-stress variations absent. Measurement omission cannot itself remove the proposed stresses and therefore is not a valid physical baseline.
